title: The coming Turkish-Israeli struggle for supremacy
gist: With Iran's proxy network collapsed, the author argues the Middle East is heading toward a Turkish-Israeli struggle for regional supremacy; Turkey, embedded in NATO and Europe with the alliance's second-largest army, is far better placed than Iran ever was to be the balancing hegemon, and an Israeli-Turkish war could fracture NATO itself.

insights.claim: With Iran's forward-positioned proxies (Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis) destroyed by Israel, the region is being set up for a Turkish-Israeli showdown as the only two actors with hegemonic ambitions.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Reframes Middle East risk from an Iran-centric to a Turkey-centric axis, a structural shift investors in regional energy, defence and shipping should reprice.
insights.quote: the collapse of Iranian forward-positioned proxies is setting the region up for the ultimate showdown between the only two actors with hegemonic ambitions
insights.locator: That the Middle East is hurtling towards

insights.claim: The view that Turkey is Iran's successor as regional balancer now shapes Israeli strategic doctrine across the political spectrum, from Netanyahu to opposition leaders like Naftali Bennett, so the conflict potential persists regardless of who governs Israel.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Signals the Turkey-Israel rivalry is a durable structural feature, not a partisan or election-dependent risk.
insights.quote: As Iran weakens, that vacuum will be filled by the natural candidate with imperial ambitions in the Middle East, and that is Turkey
insights.locator: 'As Iran weakens, that vacuum will be filled

themes.theme: Why Turkey outclasses Iran as a hegemon

insights.claim: Turkey is a far stronger candidate for regional hegemony than Iran was: it holds NATO's second-largest army and Europe's largest military, is economically entwined with Europe, and commands Sunni confidence from Egypt to Pakistan including the Gulf monarchies and Jordan.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Explains why the new balancer cannot be contained the way Iran was, raising the ceiling on regional escalation risk.
insights.quote: it has the alliance's second-largest army, after the United States, and the largest military in Europe
insights.locator: Turkey is not Iran. It westernised itself

insights.claim: Iran failed as the regional balancer because its Shia identity structurally opposed the Sunni-majority Middle East and it lacked the economic, military and demographic capacity to translate influence into sustainable hegemony.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Diagnoses why Kissinger-era realist bets on Iran-as-balancer and Obama's integration strategy failed, informing how to assess the Turkey bet.
insights.quote: Iran's Shia identity placed it in structural opposition to much of the predominantly Sunni Middle East
insights.locator: Both Waltz's theory and Obama's strategy

insights.claim: Turkey's key advantage over Iran is its acceptance inside Western institutions: embedded in NATO, economically interdependent with the EU (especially Germany), and courted by both Britain and Germany, making it politically hard for the West to contain.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Turkey can pursue regional ambition while remaining inside the Western tent, complicating any coalition to check it.
insights.quote: Turkey possesses an advantage that Iran never enjoyed: substantial political, economic and strategic acceptance in both the United States and Europe
insights.locator: And yet, as discussed, Turkey possesses

insights.claim: An emerging Saudi-Pakistani security relationship potentially brings Pakistan's nuclear deterrence into the wider strategic matrix, and a Saudi-Pakistani bloc under Ankara's hegemony could contain both Russia and Iran.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: A potential new nuclear-backed bloc reshaping the regional balance, a tail risk with major implications for proliferation and alignment.
insights.quote: an emerging Saudi-Pakistani security relationship that potentially brings Pakistan's nuclear deterrence into the wider strategic matrix
insights.locator: A recent addition has further empowered

insights.claim: The author warns that declining US support for Israel among younger Democrats and Republicans, plus a possible future Democratic administration, could make a Saudi-Pakistani bloc under Turkey appealing to Washington and leave Israel's Greece-Cyprus alignment less durable.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Flags a generational shift in US politics as a slow-moving driver that could strand Israel diplomatically, relevant to long-horizon regional bets.
insights.quote: the steadily declining support for Israel among both younger generations of Democrats and Republicans

insights.claim: The Iran War demonstrated that relatively weak states can impose effective land-based blockades on seapowers, a lesson Ankara and Beijing will have absorbed.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Undercuts the strategic value of expensive naval power projection, with implications for defence procurement and maritime chokepoint risk.
insights.quote: Iran has effectively demonstrated that relatively weak states can impose effective land-based blockades on seapowers.

insights.claim: Cheap offence exemplified by drones is now overwhelmingly influential for the first time since the tank, straining expensive defensive platforms and shifting advantage from sea-based power projection to localised land powers with cheap educated workforces and advanced technology.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: A cost-of-offence-versus-defence inversion that favours cheap-drone producers and erodes the value of legacy high-cost defence platforms.
insights.quote: Cheap offence, exemplified by drones, for the first time since the development of tanks, is now overwhelmingly influential, placing great strain on expensive defensive platforms.

insights.claim: An Israeli attack on Turkey, or an all-out Turkish-Israeli war over Syria or Cyprus, has the potential to destroy NATO as we know it by pitting a member state's defence against an Israeli action.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: The single largest tail risk in the piece: a regional war that fractures the Western alliance itself, a systemic geopolitical shock.
insights.quote: An Israeli attack on Turkey, or an all-out Turkish-Israeli war over expansionism in Syria or Cyprus, therefore has the potential to destroy NATO as we know it.
insights.locator: The United States will, of course

insights.claim: In any direct conflict Turkey holds the geographic advantage, with a million men under arms one coordinated thrust from Nazareth and Haifa, and the US would not go to war with Turkey as it might have with Iran.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Israel cannot rely on automatic US backing against a NATO ally, materially changing the deterrence calculus in the region.
insights.quote: a million Turkish men under arms would be one well-coordinated thrust away from the gates of Nazareth and Haifa
insights.locator: In any potential conflict with Israel

insights.claim: American retrenchment, whether from imperial exhaustion, debt, generational change or strategic defeat, will translate into a scramble for localised regional hegemony by ambitious powers, with Turkey returning to imperial form.
insights.speaker: Sumantra Maitra
insights.so_what: Frames US withdrawal as the meta-driver enabling regional hegemons, a structural thesis for long-term geopolitical positioning.
insights.quote: American retrenchment, either due to imperial exhaustion, debt, generational change or strategic defeat, will translate into a mad dash for localised regional hegemony
